newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS - Low prices, Copec weigh on CHH Q3.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Low prices, Copec weigh on CHH Q3.

text.p: A smaller contribution from its Chilean associate, Copec, and weak prices combined to drag Carter Holt Harvey Ltd's nine-profit down 53 percent to NZ$171 million in the nine months to December 31, CHH said on Tuesday.
The forest products group, just over half owned by International Paper, made a net profit over the December quarter of NZ$53 million, well short of analysts' expectations of around $68-76 million.
"The financial results reflect the effects of cyclical low pricing in most of the markets in which the company operates," CHH said.
"The general improvement in pricing experienced from the first to the second quarter did not continue into the third quarter, and in some cases prices reversed," it said.

The main reason for the decline in equity earnings to NZ$54 million from $131 million was a sharp fall in the contribution from its 30.05 percent indirect associate, Compania de Petroleos de Chile S.A. (Copec).
Declining pulp prices had also impacted on Copec's affiliate, Arauco, and Copec's fishing operations had suffered.

CHH's involvement with Copec has been the subject of long-running litigation with the other joint venture partner in Copec, the Angelini group. CHH has been fighting to obtain a direct stake in the company and board representation.
Chief Executive Officer John Faraci said CHH wanted to obtain rights as a major shareholder, be an active and equal partner, and to maximise synergies between the two.
The matter is to go before an aribitrator in March.

David Stanley, equity analyst at Doyle Paterson Brown, said that on an operating level, CHH's earnings were a little better than he had expected. "But where the numbers have fallen short in this quarter is through the contribution from Chile," he said. "That was something of a surprise although it is clear that pulp prices had been weakening in the last quarter."
Copec sells proportionately more of its pulp into the spot market, where prices have been falling more rapidly than in the contract market.
Faraci expected an improvement in CHH's markets over the next six to nine months and said that the company's market share in key segments remained strong.

"Over the next six to nine months an improving supply/demand situation and the benefits of the internal cost and productivity initiatives should begin to positively impact on sales and margins," he said.
Pulp price increases signalled by European and North American producers over the December quarter had mostly stalled and in some cases had reversed.
Over the near term, the outlook for pulp would remain difficult until worldwide inventory levels had fallen to more normal levels, Faraci said. To that end, CHH had cut its inventory to three weeks.

Doyle Paterson's Stanley said CHH was setting a platform for better returns as its markets improved, but added the current quarter would be a difficult one. He now expects a profit for the year of around NZ$225-230 million, against the previous year's result of $453 million.
CHH's share price dropped eight cents to NZ$3.26 after the result was announced.
